Decentralized Software

The Sovereign Code Forge: “Signed” Alpha Launches Native Git on Nostr

Moving beyond centralized web silos, reya releases a standalone collaboration platform for Nostr Git and the Grasp protocol across desktop platforms.

By reya and Staff

For years, decentralized software development has lived in a curious contradiction: developers build permissionless protocols while coordinating their code inside proprietary centralized platforms. That compromise took another step toward obsolescence today with the alpha rollout of Signed, a dedicated desktop collaboration suite built directly on Nostr Git and the Grasp Protocol.

Announcing the initial release, reya laid out a roadmap aimed at displacing commercial git hosting services with cryptographic keys and relay distribution: I've released an alpha build of "Signed", a collaboration platform for Nostr Git or Grasp Protocol. If you're bored today, please give it a try and send me some feedback or bug reports. It's still very early and rough, my vision is a fully batteries-included git client as well as a collaboration platform.

The release coincides with growing experimentation around sovereign development tooling across the network. Developer arbadacarba published both a git forge wrapper, gittr, and an Android client on Zapstore, while arguing in a separate essay that command-line interfaces should give way to sovereign graphical tools and model context integrations rather than forcing everyday developers to navigate terminal arcana.

With Signed shipping native binaries for macOS, Windows, and Linux—and a web version on the near horizon—the shift toward protocol-level code hosting is moving from an experimental curiosity into an accessible everyday reality.

Group Architecture

90s Etiquette in the Relay Age: fiatjaf Reimagines Forums for NIP-29

A text-focused topic layout in Hallway brings bulletin-board discipline and linear threading to modern Nostr groups.

By fiatjaf and Staff

As public feeds grow louder and more fragmented, protocol developers are reaching back to the architectural clarity of early web forums. Showcasing new interface work for Hallway, fiatjaf demonstrated how NIP-29 relayed groups can restore calm, topic-based discussions: Old-school text-focused forum topic list when browsing a NIP-29 group in Hallway:

Rather than adopting the infinite-scroll nesting of modern social platforms, the design consciously enforces the conversational discipline of nineties bulletin boards. Pointing out the reply flow, fiatjaf noted: In order to reply to forum topic one must go to the end of the thread, as the 90s etiquette says:

The philosophical foundation remains strict interoperability across client boundaries. In a brief remark on protocol design, fiatjaf emphasized: Interop is all that matters. Static kinds favor interop. That commitment resonated across recent group discussions, with fiatjaf adding of community collaboration tools: Thank you. I like Coop very much but it has a million bugs, so I can't use it. Now I'm hopeful the Gigi effect will make it usable for me again.

The broader push for reliable group communication was highlighted by chad, observing that Armada and Vector solve nostr DMs and make group chats possible.

Dispatch & Developments

Live Culture

Punks, Humans, and Relays: Live from the Maldon Festival

By Aaron of Essex

From a crowded hall in Essex, independent live music found an immediate, global audience without tickets or gatekeepers. Aaron of Essex reported on the second consecutive evening of festival broadcasting: The Maldon Festival Livestream was a lot of fun last night. And guess what we do it all again tonight… Join us tonight for some good old fashioned Punk and RocknRoll. With real instruments and humans.

Broadcasting over Fountain, RSS, and Nostr, the event onboarded local grassroots bands into value-for-value streaming, proving that direct audience support can fund live culture without algorithmic intermediaries.

Education

From Classroom to Bedrock: My First Bitcoin Restructures

By My First Bitcoin

In a pivotal organizational transition, My First Bitcoin announced it is shifting its primary operational focus from direct teaching to decentralized educational infrastructure.

In a formal announcement, the organization explained: My First Bitcoin is restructuring around its Education Network: a smaller team, lower costs, and a single focus—empowering those who empower others. This is how we scale the mission…

The restructuring supports over two hundred independent educators across forty-eight countries, equipping local leaders to teach Bitcoin in their native languages rather than running centralized classroom programs from a single hub.

Elsewhere on the protocol, inkan published a draft proposal for cold-storage identities on Nostr, allowing private keys to remain offline permanently while delegating daily signing capabilities to active devices.
